name: Selegiline (Emsam, Zelapar)
summary: Selegiline is an MAOI that can treat major depression (Emsam patch) and is also used in Parkinson’s disease (oral forms). In psychiatry, it’s mainly the transdermal patch for unipolar depression—powerful, but with serious interaction and safety rules.
description: Selegiline is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI). The transdermal patch (Emsam) is used for unipolar major depression in adults. It can be a good option when other antidepressants haven’t worked, but it comes with strict medication interaction rules, a suicide-risk warning for younger patients, and (at higher patch doses) dietary tyramine restrictions to avoid dangerous blood pressure spikes. Oral selegiline is primarily for Parkinson’s and has different risks and dosing.
patient_summary: Emsam (selegiline patch) is an MAOI antidepressant for adults with major depression. It can help when other meds fail, but you have to respect the rules: major drug interactions, watch closely for mood changes or suicidality (especially early), and avoid tyramine-rich foods at higher patch doses (9 or 12 mg/24 hours).

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitor; MAO-B Inhibitor (selectivity decreases with higher exposure)

linked_conditions.context: Emsam (selegiline transdermal system) is labeled for adult unipolar major depression. It’s typically considered when first-line antidepressants or therapy haven’t been enough, or when a patient needs a different mechanism and can follow MAOI safety rules.
In practice, MAOIs (including selegiline patch) often come up in treatment-resistant depression discussions because they work differently than SSRIs/SNRIs.
Selegiline is not FDA-approved for bipolar depression and can trigger mania/hypomania. Screen for bipolar disorder before starting; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to selegiline or any component of the formulation
Transdermal patch: Patients <12 years of age (increased risk of hypertensive crisis)

Transdermal patch: Use with carbamazepine, SSRIs/SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants (eg, clomipramine, imipramine), tramadol, propoxyphene, meperidine, methadone, pentazocine, and dextromethorphan (concurrently or within required washout windows)
Orally disintegrating tablet: Concomitant use or within 14 days of other MAOIs (including linezolid), opioids (eg, meperidine, methadone, tramadol), cyclobenzaprine, dextromethorphan, St. John's wort

efficacy_response.patient_text: With the patch, some people notice early changes in 1 to 2 weeks, but the more meaningful improvement usually builds across 4 to 6 weeks.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Patch provides steady delivery with higher systemic selegiline exposure and lower metabolite exposure vs oral forms; oral capsule/tablet has significant first-pass metabolism with higher metabolite exposure
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Transdermal about 73% (adult PK data); oral capsule about 4% (adult PK data)
pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: early effects may be seen in 1-2 weeks; continued improvement through 4-6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Transdermal: time to peak ~20 hours; ODT: 10-15 minutes; capsule: ~0.86 hours (adult PK data)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral: ~10 hours; transdermal: ~20 hours (adult PK data)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP2A6 (minor) to active (N-desmethylselegiline, amphetamine, methamphetamine) and inactive metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Capsule/tablet bioavailability increases 3- to 4-fold with food; ODT exposure decreases with food; patch avoids gut MAO-A inhibition relative to oral

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, selegiline matters mostly as the Emsam patch for {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:unipolar major depression} in adults. It’s an MAOI—meaning it’s not a casual “try it and see” med. It can be a strong option when other antidepressants haven’t delivered, but you have to follow strict interaction rules, and at higher patch doses you also have food rules (tyramine).
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar)}: Emsam transdermal patch in adults

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Here’s what people commonly describe—especially with the Emsam patch. Your mileage may vary.

quotes: Week 1 I wasn’t magically happy, but I felt less… stuck.
Around week 3, the heaviness started backing off.
It didn’t flip a switch. It slowly gave me more room to breathe.

items.category: Energy + activation (can be good… or too much)
quotes: My brain felt a little more ‘on’—like the fog thinned out.
I had more drive, but I had to watch for feeling wired.
I felt restless at first, like my body wanted to move.
items.note: If activation ramps into agitation, insomnia, impulsivity, or hypomania/mania symptoms, that’s not a “push through it” situation—tell your prescriber ASAP.

quotes: I slept lighter the first couple weeks.
It helped my depression but messed with my sleep at first.
Once I adjusted, sleep got more normal—but early on I had insomnia.
items.note: Insomnia is a known side effect (especially early).

quotes: The med was fine, but the patch area got red and itchy.
I had to rotate sites or my skin got angry.
The patch worked—my skin did not love it.
items.note: Application-site reactions can happen and may be common with the patch.

items.category: The MAOI rules (the mental load is real)
quotes: The med helped, but I had to become a label-reader overnight.
The drug interaction list is no joke—my pharmacist became my best friend.
I got anxious about taking cold meds because the rules are strict.
items.note: This medication has major interaction risks. Planning and communication are part of the treatment.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: This isn’t a “feel it in an hour” med. It’s an antidepressant timeline: slow, steady, and cumulative.
key_points: 1-2 weeks: Some people notice early shifts (less hopelessness, slightly more energy, less emotional “cement boots” feeling)
4-6 weeks: More complete antidepressant effect often shows up here
Patch delivery: Medication levels rise gradually and stay steadier day-to-day compared with many oral meds
Stopping: Interaction and diet restrictions can linger after discontinuation—washout rules still apply

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Clinically, the patch is considered a legitimate antidepressant option—especially when people haven’t responded to typical first-line meds. The key thing to know is that benefit is usually gradual (weeks, not hours), and safety hinges on following the interaction and (at higher doses) dietary rules.
sections.clinical_details: Early improvement may be seen in the first 1 to 2 weeks, with ongoing gains over 4 to 6 weeks. If there’s no meaningful movement after an adequate trial at an adequate dose—while following washout rules and avoiding contraindicated meds—your prescriber usually reassesses the plan.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This is an MAOI. Drug interactions can be dangerous. At higher patch doses (9 or 12 mg/24h), tyramine foods can trigger a hypertensive crisis.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
other: Age restriction (patch): Contraindicated in patients <12 years due to increased risk of hypertensive crisis
Mania/hypomania risk (patch): Can trigger a switch in people with bipolar disorder; screen before starting

Serotonin syndrome risk: Can happen with serotonergic meds (SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, triptans, fentanyl, lithium, buspirone, St. John’s wort, tryptophan) or other MAOIs (including linezolid and IV methylene blue)
Hypertensive crisis risk: Especially with tyramine-rich foods at patch doses ≥9 mg/24 hours, or with interacting meds
CNS impairment: Can cause drowsiness and impair driving/operating machinery; sudden sleep episodes have been reported (notably with orally disintegrating tablets)
Blood pressure effects: Can worsen hypertension or cause orthostatic hypotension—monitor especially during titration and in older adults
Psychosis/hallucinations (notably oral forms used in Parkinson’s): Can worsen mental status; avoid in major psychotic disorders
Heat warning (patch): Heat exposure (heating pads, saunas, hot tubs, prolonged sunlight) can increase absorption
patient_counseling: If you’re under 25—or you have a history of suicidality—expect closer check-ins early on. If suicidal thoughts worsen, don’t white-knuckle it. Call your prescriber urgently.
Do not mix this medication with contraindicated antidepressants, stimulants, dextromethorphan, tramadol, meperidine, methadone, or other listed interacting meds. Washout periods matter.
If you’re on 9 mg/24h or 12 mg/24h patches: you’ll need tyramine food restrictions starting day 1, and they continue for 2 weeks after stopping or dropping back to 6 mg/24h.
Know hypertensive crisis red flags: sudden severe headache, chest pain, stiff neck, nausea/vomiting, sweating, palpitations, or a sudden spike in blood pressure—seek emergency care.
Tell your prescriber about every OTC med and supplement—especially cold/cough products, decongestants, and herbal blends.
Rotate patch sites; don’t apply to irritated or broken skin; avoid external heat on or near the patch.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common themes: patch site reactions (patch), insomnia/headache/dizziness, nausea, and blood pressure changes. Some people can feel activated or agitated—especially early or with dose changes.
plain_language_list: Skin irritation where the patch sits (redness, itching)

common.patient_note: Redness or irritation where the patch sits is common. Rotating sites and applying to clean, dry, intact skin helps. If you get blistering, ulcers, or severe rash, tell your prescriber.

Headache can happen, especially early. If headache is sudden and severe—especially with chest pain, palpitations, sweating, or nausea—treat it like a hypertensive crisis warning sign and seek urgent help.
Sleep can get rocky at first. If insomnia is severe, your prescriber may adjust timing, address sleep hygiene, or reassess the dose.
Standing up too fast can hit like a wave. Hydrate, rise slowly, and report fainting or frequent dizziness—especially if you’re older or on blood pressure meds.
Nausea is fairly common. If you can’t keep food down or it’s persistent, tell your prescriber.
Dizziness can be from blood pressure shifts or CNS effects. Avoid driving until you know how you respond.

serious: Hypertensive crisis: severe headache, dangerously high blood pressure, chest pain, palpitations, sweating, nausea/vomiting—medical emergency
Serotonin syndrome: agitation/confusion, sweating, fever, tremor/rigidity, diarrhea, labile blood pressure—medical emergency
Mania/hypomania: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, irritability, grandiosity—urgent reassessment needed
Psychosis/hallucinations (more noted with oral formulations in Parkinson’s): paranoia, delusions, severe confusion—urgent evaluation
Suicidal ideation or abrupt worsening depression—urgent evaluation

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: This is the part you do not wing. Selegiline (especially the antidepressant patch) has major interaction risks. Some combos can trigger serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis.

items.with: Other antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs like clomipramine/imipramine) and other MAOIs
items.risk: Serotonin syndrome and other serious toxicity; some combinations are contraindicated.
items.action: Follow washout rules. In general: wait 14 days between stopping most antidepressants/MAOIs and starting selegiline, and wait 14 days after stopping selegiline before starting another antidepressant/MAOI. Fluoxetine requires a longer washout (5 weeks) before starting selegiline.

items.with: Opioids (especially meperidine; also methadone, tramadol; certain opioid-like meds)
items.risk: Severe, potentially fatal reactions; multiple opioids are contraindicated depending on formulation.
items.action: Avoid contraindicated opioids. Tell every clinician you’re on an MAOI before receiving pain meds or anesthesia.

items.risk: Serious CNS toxicity and serotonin syndrome risk; contraindicated with certain formulations and timing windows.
items.action: Avoid dextromethorphan products unless your prescriber explicitly clears it.

items.with: St. John’s wort, tryptophan, and other serotonergic supplements
items.action: Avoid unless specifically approved by your prescriber.

items.risk: Significant interaction risk listed as contraindicated for transdermal system.
Hypertensive crisis, especially at 9 mg/24h and 12 mg/24h patch doses.
items.action: At doses ≥9 mg/24h: avoid tyramine-rich foods and drinks starting day 1 and continuing for 2 weeks after stopping or reducing to 6 mg/24h.

items.risk: MAOIs have special anesthesia rules; some manufacturers list use within 10 days of elective surgery as contraindicated due to interaction risks.
items.action: Coordinate with psychiatry + anesthesia. If continued, use an MAOI-safe anesthetic plan (avoid meperidine and indirect-acting adrenergic agonists).

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on the antidepressant patch for 4+ weeks, don’t just rip it off and hope for the best. MAOIs can come with more intense discontinuation symptoms in some people, so tapering tends to be more conservative.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over about 2 to 4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and catch returning depression early
If treatment lasted 2 to 3 weeks: taper over 1 to 2 weeks may be reasonable
If treatment lasted <2 weeks: tapering often isn’t necessary, but clinical judgment still applies
Go slower (eg, ≥4 weeks) if you’ve had withdrawal issues before or you’re on higher doses
Some long-term patients (>6 months), especially with a history of discontinuation syndrome, may do better tapering over >3 months
If withdrawal becomes intolerable: return to the prior dose and taper more slowly

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatry dosing here focuses on the transdermal patch for unipolar major depression. The patch is changed once daily. Dose changes are slow (every 2 weeks) so your brain can catch up and so side effects don’t get out of hand.

adult.depression_patch_initial: Apply 6 mg/24 hours transdermal patch once daily
adult.depression_patch_titration: If needed based on response/tolerability, increase by 3 mg/24 hours increments every 2 weeks

sections.simple_explanation: Most people start and stay at 6 mg/24 hours. If symptoms aren’t improving enough, the dose can be raised slowly—usually every 2 weeks. At 9 mg/24 hours and 12 mg/24 hours, tyramine food restrictions become important to reduce hypertensive crisis risk.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: For depression, pregnancy and breastfeeding data are limited, so other options are often preferred unless there’s a clear reason to use selegiline. Age matters a lot with the patch: it’s contraindicated under age 12.
sections.pregnancy: Information on selegiline use in pregnancy is limited. For major depression in pregnancy, other treatments are often preferred unless benefits clearly outweigh risks and alternatives aren’t appropriate.
sections.lactation: It’s not known whether selegiline is present in breast milk. Because of potential serious adverse reactions in a breastfeeding infant, the manufacturer does not recommend breastfeeding while on selegiline. If selegiline is stopped, guidance suggests waiting 5 days after the final patch is removed before breastfeeding.
sections.pediatrics: Patch is contraindicated in children <12 years due to increased risk of hypertensive crisis. Adolescents >17 years may use the patch per adult dosing when clinically appropriate, with close monitoring for suicidality and mood activation.
sections.geriatrics: For depression with the patch: 6 mg/24 hours once daily is commonly used. Older adults may have higher exposure and may be more sensitive to blood pressure changes (orthostasis) and CNS effects; monitor closely.
sections.hepatic: Patch: Mild to moderate impairment (Child-Pugh A/B): no adjustment necessary. Severe impairment (Child-Pugh C): no specific patch adjustment provided in labeling (not well studied); use caution. Oral ODT has specific limits (not recommended in Child-Pugh C), but that’s typically Parkinson-focused dosing.
sections.renal: Patch: eGFR ≥15 mL/minute/1.73 m2: no adjustment necessary. eGFR <15 or ESRD: no specific adjustment provided in labeling (not studied); use caution.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood and behavior changes: worsening depression, irritability, agitation, panic symptoms, insomnia, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania—especially during the first 1-2 months and when the dose changes
Suicidal ideation and behaviors: close monitoring in pediatric and young adult patients and anyone with past suicidality, especially early in treatment and around dose increases/decreases
Blood pressure: watch for new or worsening hypertension, orthostatic hypotension, and any signs suggesting hypertensive crisis
Serotonin syndrome symptoms if any serotonergic exposure occurs: mental status changes, autonomic instability, tremor/rigidity, GI symptoms, seizures—stop meds and seek urgent care if suspected
Sleep: insomnia vs daytime sleepiness; assess safety for driving and tasks requiring alertness
Patch site skin checks: irritation, rash, ulceration; confirm site rotation and proper application technique
Medication and supplement reconciliation at every visit: OTC cold/cough meds, herbal supplements, new prescriptions from other clinicians

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Selegiline comes in multiple formulations, but for psychiatry the main one is the Emsam patch. The oral forms are mostly Parkinson-focused.
items: Transdermal patch (Emsam): 6 mg/24 hr, 9 mg/24 hr, 12 mg/24 hr
Orally disintegrating tablet (Zelapar): 1.25 mg (contains aspartame; grapefruit flavor)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Selegiline blocks monoamine oxidase (MAO), an enzyme that breaks down brain chemicals like dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin. At lower exposure it leans more toward MAO-B inhibition, but that selectivity can fade as exposure increases. With the antidepressant patch, blood levels are higher and MAO effects are broader, which is part of why it can work for depression—and also why interaction and (at higher doses) diet rules matter.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Emsam sits in the “powerful but rules-heavy” corner of depression treatment. It’s not usually a first pick for mild depression. It becomes more relevant when depression is persistent, recurrent, or not responding well to standard options—and when someone can reliably follow MAOI safety rules (interaction checks, washout periods, and tyramine restrictions at higher doses). It also matters in complex cases where side effect profiles of SSRIs/SNRIs aren’t a fit. The big clinical job is screening for bipolar disorder, planning interactions and washouts, and monitoring early for agitation, insomnia, and suicidality.

seo.title: Selegiline (Emsam, Zelapar): Uses, Dosing, Interactions, Tyramine Diet & Safety
seo.description: Selegiline (Emsam patch) is an MAOI antidepressant for unipolar major depression in adults. Learn dosing (6–12 mg/24h), washout rules, dangerous interactions, tyramine diet at higher doses, side effects, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is selegiline (Emsam) used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, the big use is Emsam—the selegiline transdermal patch—for unipolar major depressive disorder in adults. It’s an MAOI antidepressant, which means it has stricter safety rules than most antidepressants, especially around drug interactions and (at higher doses) diet.

faqs.q: How long does the Emsam patch take to work?
faqs.a: It’s not instant. Some people notice early shifts in 1 to 2 weeks, but the more meaningful improvement often builds over 4 to 6 weeks.

faqs.q: What’s the starting dose for the selegiline patch?
faqs.a: For adult unipolar depression, the usual starting (and often target) dose is 6 mg/24 hours—one patch daily. If needed, the dose can be increased by 3 mg/24 hours every 2 weeks up to 12 mg/24 hours.

faqs.q: Do I have to avoid certain foods on Emsam?
faqs.a: It depends on the dose. At 6 mg/24 hours, tyramine restrictions are generally less of an issue. At 9 mg/24 hours and 12 mg/24 hours, you should avoid tyramine-rich foods and beverages starting day 1, and keep avoiding them for 2 weeks after stopping the patch or dropping back down to 6 mg/24 hours. This helps prevent hypertensive crisis.

faqs.q: What foods are considered high in tyramine?
faqs.a: Classic examples include aged cheeses, air-dried or cured meats (like salami), some fermented soy products (like soy sauce), sauerkraut, and tap/draft beers. Food freshness matters too—spoiled or improperly stored foods can have higher tyramine.

faqs.q: What medications can’t be taken with selegiline?
faqs.a: Many. Big red flags include SSRIs/SNRIs, certain tricyclics (like clomipramine), other MAOIs (including linezolid), dextromethorphan (common in cough syrups), tramadol, meperidine, methadone, and St. John’s wort. Your prescriber and pharmacist should review every prescription, OTC med, and supplement before you take it.

faqs.q: What are the washout periods when switching antidepressants with selegiline?
faqs.a: In general, allow 14 days between stopping most antidepressants (or other MAOIs) and starting selegiline, and allow 14 days after stopping selegiline before starting another antidepressant or MAOI. Fluoxetine is the exception—because it hangs around longer, you typically wait 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting selegiline.

Like other antidepressants, it carries a warning that short-term studies showed increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients. That’s why close monitoring early in treatment—and during dose changes—matters, especially if you’re under 25 or have a history of suicidality.

Yes. The patch can precipitate mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. That’s why clinicians screen for bipolar disorder before starting, and why antidepressant monotherapy is generally avoided in bipolar illness.

faqs.q: What are signs of hypertensive crisis on an MAOI?
faqs.a: Think: sudden severe headache, chest pain, palpitations, sweating, nausea/vomiting, stiff neck, or a sudden spike in blood pressure. If that happens, treat it as an emergency.

faqs.q: How should I apply the Emsam patch?
faqs.a: Apply to clean, dry, intact skin on the upper torso (below the neck, above the waist), upper thigh, or outer upper arm. Rotate sites, don’t put it under tight clothing, wash hands after handling, and avoid heat sources (heating pads, saunas, hot tubs, prolonged direct sunlight) near the patch area.

faqs.q: How do I stop the selegiline patch safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4+ weeks, tapering over about 2 to 4 weeks is commonly recommended to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to catch returning depression early. If you get significant discontinuation symptoms, the usual move is to go back to the prior dose and taper more slowly.
